dossier.headline: A megacity draining its aquifer on an old lakebed — the drying climate tightens the squeeze.

sections.title: What we observed
sections.body: NISAR L-band's first look (Oct 2025 – Jan 2026) mapped neighborhoods sinking more than 2 cm per month; historical peak rates reached ~35 cm/yr in the 1990s–2000s. The mechanism is published and long-established: groundwater pumping under the clays of ancient Lake Texcoco.

sections.title: What it means
sections.body: Like the Central Valley, this is aquifer compaction — but under one of the world's largest cities, so the damage shows up as cracked metro lines, broken pipes and leaning buildings. Climate change deepens the driver: longer droughts push the city to pump more, while harder rains must drain through a distorted, sinking system.

sections.title: What the evidence cannot tell us
sections.body: How much subsidence recent management actions have avoided; the exact compaction split between depth layers; and how NISAR's early 2025–2026 rates compare to historical peaks without the same processing chain. This app's scene is a physics rendering tuned to published figures — not raw SAR pixels.

interpretation.public: Mexico City sits on the clay of an ancient lake and drinks from the aquifer below it. Every liter pumped lets the clay compress a little, and the city sinks — over 2 cm in a month in the newest radar maps. Droughts make cities pump harder, so a hotter, drier climate turns directly into sinking streets and broken pipes.
interpretation.student: Pumping lowers water pressure in the aquifer, and the soft lakebed clays compact — mostly permanently. NISAR (L-band radar, launched 2024–25) mapped sinking above 2 cm/month in Oct 2025–Jan 2026; historical peaks hit ~35 cm/yr. The same physics as the Central Valley case, but the 'infrastructure' being deformed is a megacity.
interpretation.scientist: InSAR time series (NISAR L-band, Oct 2025–Jan 2026; historical SBAS studies) resolve differential settlement up to >2 cm/mo over compressible Texcoco lakebed clays, consistent with decades of published rates (~5–35 cm/yr) driven by heads decline from aquifer extraction. In-app scene: analytic bowl (MODELED), peak 30 cm over a 360-day window.

dataset.mission: NISAR L-band (2025–26 first look); historical Sentinel-1/Envisat/ERS for published series
dataset.datasetId: NASA/JPL NISAR early results; published InSAR literature rates
dataset.window: Published: Oct 2025 – Jan 2026 NISAR look; historical 1990s–2020s series; in-app pass-pair window: 360 days
dataset.coverage: Mexico City metro on the former Lake Texcoco bed (~55 km scene)
dataset.gnss: Not bundled for this event — published rates cited instead; regional CORS coverage is sparse relative to the deformation gradient
dataset.processing: Published: multi-mission InSAR time series. In-app: analytic elastic bowl model tuned to the published peak rates; one fringe = λ/2 line-of-sight motion

items.label: MEASURED
items.detail: >2 cm/mo mapped by NISAR L-band (Oct 2025–Jan 2026, NASA/JPL) and ~35 cm/yr historical peaks. Shown as citations; not re-derived in-app.

items.label: MODELED
items.detail: Physics rendering of an elastic bowl source (peak 30 cm over the 360-day window) tuned to published rates. NOT a raw SAR image — computed on-device.

items.label: DERIVED
items.detail: Computed on-device from the physical model (one fringe = λ/2 LOS). Tracks the model, not a downloaded product.

items.label: LIVE
items.detail: Live accelerometer from the demo ESP32 ground station — IoT demo at the demo site; not a satellite measurement of this event.

limitations: The interferogram is a physics rendering of published figures, not raw SAR pixels — no SAR processing is done in-app.
No bundled GNSS chart for this event; cited rates come from the published literature.
Depth-partitioned compaction and management effects are not resolved by this evidence.
